# In Praise of the Wrong Turn

The first time I got lost on purpose, I was trying to buy a lemon. Our route to the grocery store was six blocks long, a line I could have drawn blindfolded. That morning I detoured because a bakery had appeared on a side street, its sign handwritten and its windows fogged with warmth. I remembered thinking: a lemon can wait. Twenty minutes later, I was standing beneath a railway bridge, holding an empty paper bag, unsure which direction home lay. The bakery had led me into a neighborhood whose streets seemed assembled by several different people. Nothing was wrong, exactly. I simply knew less than I thought.

A wrong turn is ordinarily a failure of method. You meant to go north, and now you are south; you meant to arrive at four, and now you are late. We are taught to regard these outcomes as evidence of carelessness, minor embarrassments to be corrected before anyone notices. Yet there is a peculiar pleasure in becoming briefly unfamiliar with a place. Familiarity is comfortable, but it can also become a kind of blindness. We see the grocery store without seeing the pharmacy beside it, pass the same garden without noticing its first green shoots, and travel through our own lives using a map drawn long ago.

As children, we understood getting lost differently. For adults, it is usually an inconvenience involving directions, traffic, and the possibility of embarrassment. For children, it can be an expansion of the world. A street that looked like the way home might turn out to lead to a construction site, a creek, or the mysterious fence belonging to somebody who did not want to be found. Children do not necessarily experience this as anxiety. They have not yet formed a fixed idea of what the route ought to be, so the wrong turn remains an available possibility rather than a deviation from a plan.

Paper maps made getting lost more visually obvious. I remember studying one as a boy, tracing my finger along the blue line of a road while riding in the back seat. The map promised a tidy arrangement of streets, though the actual neighborhood contained extra paths, alleys, and pathways across vacant lots. A route on paper might show a direct connection that did not exist. A building drawn at one scale might stand three stories away. My finger traveled confidently through a world made of symbols, while the landscape outside insisted on its complications.

The paper map also had a politics. It made some roads grand and others nearly invisible. Railways appeared as sharp black lines, while footpaths sometimes disappeared altogether. Parks became green spaces, but only after their muddy interiors had been edited away. A child could easily believe that the map was the territory itself, and that turning the paper in the wrong direction somehow turned the town with it. I learned to distrust that confidence. A map is useful precisely because it leaves things out, but its omissions are not always marked clearly enough.

Electronic maps changed the experience without eliminating uncertainty. A little arrow now tells us when to turn, and a blue circle announces that we have arrived. This is wonderful when the signal is clear and frustrating when it is not. The device may confidently instruct us to cross a road, then abruptly lose connection at the exact moment we need guidance. It can calculate a route around traffic while sending us into a labyrinth of one-way streets. Technology does not remove the possibility of getting lost; it merely changes the voice of the instruction.

There is something revealing about being beyond the signal. Without the little arrow, we must look again. We begin to notice the direction of shadows, the position of the sun, the slope of a hill, the sound of traffic. A street that seemed meaningless acquires a front and a back. We start using our eyes for more than identification. A yellow house becomes a landmark. A broken pickup truck parked at the corner becomes a reference point. The city stops being a sequence of destinations and becomes a place with a texture.

Asking for directions is one of the easiest ways to recover. “Excuse me, where am I?” The question is small, but it requires a person to set aside the performance of knowing. We may pretend to consult a phone, or study a storefront as though it were written in a language we understand. Eventually we admit that the black box cannot help. A stranger may point toward a distant church steeple, mention a pharmacy, or warn us that the shortcut ends at a wall. Their knowledge is local, imperfect, and occasionally contradictory, but it is enough to give the next turn a shape.

The information we receive is not always accurate. Someone may remember the old name of a road, describe a route that has changed, or point confidently toward the wrong railway station. This is not a failure of the encounter. It means that directions belong to a moving world. A place is not a fixed diagram but a temporary agreement among its residents, buildings, weather, and habits. The person giving directions is not supplying a perfect map; they are sharing the version they know.

Strangers also know things that official systems overlook. They know which bench stays dry in the rain, which shortcut is safe after dark, and which shopkeeper will let someone wait inside while a storm passes. They know why a certain road is closed, though they do not always know when it will reopen. Their knowledge is unofficial, but that does not make it inferior. Indeed, a city can be understood most accurately through its unofficial histories: the place where someone once waited for a bus, the corner where a dog was found, the house with the blue door that everyone uses as a meeting point.

This does not mean that getting lost is automatically instructive. Sometimes the wrong turn leads to a dead end behind a loading dock. Sometimes it costs us an hour we did not have, or leaves us stranded somewhere uncomfortable. The lesson of a wrong turn is not that every detour is secretly valuable. A closed gate remains closed. A flooded underpass remains dangerous. We should be able to acknowledge inconvenience without turning it into a moral lesson, and appreciate a useful mistake without pretending that all mistakes are useful.

I once watched a man ask for directions while holding a small paper map upside down. He had been given the map by his daughter before a long journey, and he was determined to follow it faithfully. A woman passing by corrected his orientation, studied the route, and then admitted that she was not familiar with the part of town he needed to reach. For a moment they stood together, examining the map. Then he folded it carefully and thanked her. The exchange had not solved his problem, but it had turned an individual error into a shared joke. They were both lost, and for a minute that was enough.

There is a kind of hospitality in uncertainty. It allows us to recognize another person’s confusion without ranking it above our own cleverness. The person who knows the route is not automatically more important than the person who does not. The confident traveler and the hesitant stranger share the same basic condition: they are trying to understand a place that does not entirely reveal itself. Sometimes all we can offer is a direction. Sometimes the kindest thing is to admit that we are lost too.

Getting lost can also mean losing track of time. When the phone stops guiding us, the afternoon becomes less structured. A ten-minute errand may expand into an hour, or an hour may pass before we realize it. We notice hunger, then postponement, then a stronger hunger. We see a shop we have never entered. We follow a sound, a smell, a patch of light. Without the pressure of the intended destination, the mind becomes less like a list and more like a room in which objects have been moved around. A strange street can suddenly seem more interesting than the appointment we were late for.

This temporal drift is part of the appeal. Efficiency is valuable, but it can make our days feel like narrow corridors, each activity placed in its proper sequence. A wrong turn gives the corridor a window. We step outside and see that the day contains more than we planned. The bakery, the railway bridge, the empty paper bag: these are not efficient solutions, but they make a larger world available. They restore a little mystery to a place that had become familiar mainly through repetition.

Attention is the real resource of getting lost. Many people are geographically lost but mentally elsewhere, staring at a phone while missing the street around them. The opposite can happen when we stop relying entirely on a screen. Suddenly the number of doors matters. The difference between a painted curb and an unpainted one becomes important. We notice where people pause, where they cross, where they look uncertain. A place reveals itself as a network of small decisions rather than a background we pass through.

I have found that the most interesting streets are often the ones that seem least important on a map. A road without a name, a gap between buildings, a path beside a stream: these spaces resist easy description. They may look insignificant from a distance, but they can contain the details that tell us how a neighborhood actually lives. A chair outside a door suggests that someone likes to sit there. Herbs on a windowsill suggest cooking, or memory, or both. A painted arrow pointing nowhere may be a child’s joke, an old advertisement, or evidence of a story that has been forgotten.

The weather makes a familiar place strange again. Fog erases the far end of a street. Rain changes the color of every wall. Snow turns a modest path into a landscape, hiding the boundaries between sidewalk and road. In these conditions, navigation becomes a negotiation with visibility. We may know that the church is north of us, but we cannot see the steeple. We may remember that the river lies beyond the park, but the path is hidden under white. The map remains correct, but the landmarks have temporarily disappeared.

There are also wrong turns that involve no movement at all. We may be exactly where we meant to be and still feel lost, surrounded by familiar objects that fail to answer the question we are carrying. This is the existential version of the mistake, less dramatic than a railway bridge and often more difficult to explain. A person can be surrounded by people and feel entirely absent from the moment. A successful day can leave us wondering whether we have actually gone anywhere. The map says we arrived. It says nothing about what the journey meant.

Perhaps this is why the wrong turn continues to fascinate us. It is a modest form of freedom. For a little while, we are released from the obligation to know what comes next. We can follow a dog, inspect a tree, or choose the street with better light. The destination has not ceased to matter, but it no longer dominates the landscape. A different possibility has entered, and the world has become wide enough to contain it.

The surprise is that the detour often teaches us something we could not have learned by obeying the route. We discover that the neighborhood is larger than we thought. We find a shop, a bench, a view, or a conversation that we would have missed. The main road was not the only way through town. Nor was it necessarily the best. The route that looked shortest on the map may have been the least memorable. The route that added minutes gave the mind something to do besides hurry.

There is a practical wisdom in leaving room for this. When we build our days around the shortest path between obligations, we may save minutes and lose the texture of living in between. The extra block can be the difference between seeing a person and merely passing them. The delayed train can allow a thought to finish. The unexpected closure can turn an ordinary afternoon into an unplanned memory. Convenience is not an enemy, but it should not be allowed to become the only way we experience the world.

Creativity, too, depends partly on not knowing the answer in advance. A blank page produces the same blankness whether we greet it with confidence or terror. A new neighborhood can be flattened into a familiar route after a few visits, but the first walk has the generosity of a question. What is around this corner? What will this street sound like at night? Which direction will the wind change? When we cannot answer, we are more likely to look. The wrong turn is a small rehearsal for this kind of curiosity.

I do not mean to suggest that confusion is always better than clarity. Clarity can be a form of care. Someone who knows which road is flooded, which door is locked, or which train has been canceled can protect others from unnecessary trouble. The point is not that knowledge is bad. The point is that knowledge and attention should not be confused. We can know the route and still fail to see the place. We can carry a map and remain unaware of the person who needs directions beside us.

A useful wrong turn is usually followed by a return. This is important. Freedom does not require abandoning the destination forever. We can wander and still come back; we can learn the route without insisting that it was there all along. The return journey may even feel different from the outward one. Familiar landmarks have acquired new meanings. The bakery is no longer merely a place where we bought bread. It is the place where the afternoon changed direction. The railway bridge becomes a reference point for stories that would otherwise float without a location.

Sometimes the return takes longer than expected. The bus does not come. The street has been closed for a parade. We sit on a curb and watch strangers carry a large papier-mâché moon through the neighborhood. The delay is inconvenient, but it gives us a story that the efficient route could never have provided. We did not choose the parade, exactly, but we became available to it. A little disruption created a little openness.

The best wrong turns are not necessarily the most dramatic. They may involve turning left instead of right at a familiar intersection, or entering a park by the wrong gate. They may happen because we forgot to load a map, misplaced a key, or followed a child walking in an intriguing direction. Their scale is part of their appeal. They remind us that life does not become meaningful only when it reaches a large event or a distant country. Meaning can accumulate in the small act of going around the block and discovering that you were wrong about what was there.

At night, the wrong turn grows more interesting and more dangerous. Familiar streets lose their daytime details. A doorway becomes a black rectangle. A path disappears into shadow. The moon is useful, but it offers no address. We must decide whether to trust memory, watch for landmarks, or admit that we should ask someone. Darkness is a good teacher of proportion: it makes us take seriously the small things that would otherwise seem beneath notice. A lit window, a painted step, a tree leaning against a fence—each can become a guide.

There is a reason we tell stories about lost travelers. The traveler is suspended between the place they know and the place they have not yet understood. He is neither entirely at home nor entirely away. The story gives him a map, a horse, a lantern, a mysterious inn, or a road that seems to contradict itself. Maps themselves are stories. They include an argument about what deserves to be seen. The line of a road implies a history of movement; a blank area may indicate ignorance rather than emptiness. A map is made by someone who chose a center, a scale, and a set of names. When we use it, we inherit that viewpoint without always realizing it. Getting lost can expose the gaps in the story. It shows us what the map excluded, and it forces us to decide whether the exclusion was accurate.

This is one reason I distrust the fantasy in which every wrong turn is a gift from the universe. Sometimes the universe has simply blocked a road. Sometimes our sense of direction is poor. Sometimes the path is dangerous and the best decision is to turn around. Curiosity is valuable, but it should not be used to excuse poor judgment. A person who wanders deliberately can still check the weather, carry water, tell someone where they are going, and respect the boundaries of a place they do not know.

Still, I keep returning to the pleasure of uncertainty. Not because uncertainty is comfortable, but because it interrupts the ordinary assumption that the world will always be arranged around our plans. A closed road forces an adjustment. A new street asks for a response. A person asking for directions reminds us that knowledge is shared rather than privately owned. These are modest disruptions, but they reveal how much of our day is governed by habits we no longer notice.

If I could choose one habit for the coming week, it would be this: take one route without trying to optimize it. Walk without measuring the time. Leave the familiar road at the first interesting sign. Do not turn the wrong turn into a lesson immediately. Buy the lemon after the detour, not before. Notice the bakery’s name, the smell of the coffee shop, the way the pavement slopes toward the river. Return when it is convenient, not when the schedule demands it.

The point is not to be lost forever. The point is to make room for a little uncertainty before everything becomes routine. We already know where the grocery store is. We know the answer to many practical questions. Somewhere between those answers, however, the day becomes interesting. A wrong turn is one way to reach that space. It is a small breach in the wall of certainty, and through it we may glimpse not only another street but another way of paying attention.
